questions.stem: A person pushes a wall with a force of 50 N. According to Newton's Third Law, what force does the wall exert on the person?

options.text: 0 N — the wall does not push back
25 N in the opposite direction
50 N in the opposite direction
100 N in the opposite direction

questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The wall pushes back on the person with exactly 50 N in the opposite direction. The forces are always equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. They act on different objects — one on the wall, one on the person.

questions.stem: A swimmer pushes backward on the water with her hands. What happens according to Newton's Third Law?

options.text: The water pushes her forward with an equal force
The water pushes her backward with an equal force
The water does not exert any force on her
The water pushes her forward with a larger force

questions.explanation: When the swimmer pushes backward on the water, the water pushes forward on the swimmer with an equal and opposite force. This forward force from the water propels the swimmer. Option (b) has the wrong direction — the reaction force is opposite to the action. Option (d) violates Newton's Third Law — the forces must be equal.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct Newton's Third Law force pair?

options.text: The weight of a book and the normal force from the table
The weight of a book and the gravitational pull of the book on the Earth
Friction on a tyre and the driving force of the engine
Air resistance on a car and the weight of the car

questions.explanation: A Newton's Third Law pair must: (1) be equal in magnitude, (2) be opposite in direction, (3) act on different objects, and (4) be the same type of force. The Earth pulls the book down (gravity), and the book pulls the Earth up (gravity) — same type of force, different objects. Option (a) is a common misconception: weight and normal force act on the same object and are different types of force.

questions.stem: A rocket expels exhaust gases downward with a force of 20 000 N. What force do the gases exert on the rocket?

options.text: 0 N — the gases just escape
20 000 N downward
20 000 N upward
Less than 20 000 N upward, due to gravity

questions.explanation: By Newton's Third Law, the rocket pushes the gases down with 20 000 N, and the gases push the rocket up with 20 000 N. These are equal and opposite forces on different objects. Option (d) is wrong — the Third Law pair is always exactly equal regardless of gravity. Gravity is a separate force that acts on the rocket in addition to the thrust.

questions.stem: If the action and reaction forces in Newton's Third Law are always equal and opposite, why don't they cancel out?

options.text: They do cancel out, which is why nothing ever moves
The reaction force is slightly smaller than the action force
They act on different objects, so they cannot cancel each other
They only cancel out when the objects are the same mass

questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law force pairs act on different objects. Forces can only cancel when they act on the same object. For example, when you push a trolley, you exert a force on the trolley and the trolley exerts an equal force on you — but these act on different bodies, so they don't cancel. The trolley accelerates because the force on it may be unbalanced.
